posts.text: ...Alderman appears under his Indian name on deeds in Plymouth County, where he had at least 3 children. One of his grandchildren, John Thomas who died in 1803 identified Alderman as his grandfather. He had been given land in Westport, MA but he sold it to a white man from Portsmouth and moved.

Martha Simon was interviewed by none other than Henry David Thoreau in his diaries. She was living in a wigwam at the end of Sconticut Neck and there was a big pile of clam shells outside the house. The Indians of Sakonnet changed their land at Little Compton for 20 acres in Fairhaven.

Martha Simon lived on Sconticut Neck over New Bedford and in Middleboro or Lakeville, MA. She was a descendant of John and William Simon, Indian ministers from Little Compton. The last Indian land was sold at Little Compton and exchanged for land at "Wigwam Road" in Fairhaven, MA.

The "Brown Lady", believed to haunt Raynham Hall, Norfolk, England.Her name Is from the brown brocade dress she is reported to wear.She gained global fame in 1936 when photographers from Country Life magazine captured a translucent shape descending the estate's grand staircase.
posts.imageAlt: The image, taken long before the invention of color film, is primarily a stark contrast between the darker shadows on the stairs and reflections of light. The central focus, however, is a vaguely human-shaped area right in the center of the stairs that appears indistinct, but clearly differentiated from the mere reflection of light elsewhere in the frame. Though debunkers have noted that the film could simply have captured a person who moved through the frame in time-lapse, the examples they produce tend to be much clearer and well defined. John Paul Jones was an officer on the Alfred in 1776 when the ship attacked New Providence in the Bahamas capturing a number of cannon and a supply of gunpowder. When the building of Fort Phoenix in Fairhaven, MA, was completed in 1777 it was outfitted with some of the captured guns. This one survived a British raid on the harbor in 1778, when the fort was captured. It is now referred to as the "John Paul Jones cannon."
